Peder Laurentsen
pay'der low'rent-sen
n. (Danish reformer of Malmo, c. 1490–1552; author of the Malmo Book, the first sustained Danish defence of the Reformation)
From Danish Laurentsen, son of Laurents, Latin Laurentius, crowned with laurel.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Peder Laurentsen was the pen of the Danish Reformation. A canon who turned evangelical, he led the reforming party at Malmo with Claus Mortensen and Frands Vormordsen, and in 1530 he published the book by which the Danish cause first argued for itself: the Malmo Book, a full defence of what the Malmo congregation had done in abolishing the mass, dissolving the cloisters, and ordering worship in Danish. It is a work of controversy in the best sense. It does not plead for toleration; it states the case from Scripture and invites refutation. Laurentsen also wrote on the Lord's Supper against the Roman sacrifice, and he spent his later years as a schoolmaster in the city he had helped reform. The dictionary records him because he answers a persistent error about the Reformation, that it was a movement of rebellion which argued afterwards. At Malmo the argument came with the act and was published for all to read. Jude requires exactly this of the whole church, that believers “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and the faith contended for is a deposit already given, not a position being invented.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to contend as to strive in opposition or in debate; defence as that which opposes attack or injury; and an apology as a defence, something said or written in vindication of what others think wrong.

expand to see more

CONTEND, v.i. [L. contendo.] To strive; to struggle in opposition; to strive in debate; to dispute earnestly.

DEFENCE, n. [L. defensio.] That which opposes attack, violence, danger or injury; any thing that secures the person, the rights or the possessions of men.

APOLOGY, n. [Gr.] A defense; an excuse; something said or written in defense or extenuation of what appears to others wrong.

REASON, v.i. [L. ratio.] To argue; to infer conclusions from premises; to debate; to discourse by way of argument.

Key Scripture

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

1Pe 3:15 — "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:"

Php 1:17 — "But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel."

Act 17:2 — "And Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures,"

Modern Corruption

Author of the Malmo Book, 1530, in which the Danish Reformation first argued its own case from Scripture.

expand to see more

The live corruption is the conviction that doctrine should not be argued. A church persuaded that contending is in itself unkind will give up every doctrine it cannot defend without discomfort, and will mistake its own silence for charity. Laurentsen's generation had no such illusion. They printed their reasons, named their opponents, and submitted the whole to the judgment of Scripture, which is what a confessional church does when it is healthy.

The principle to recover is that the defence of the faith is a duty laid on every believer and not only on the learned. Peter requires a reason and prescribes the manner of giving it: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15), with meekness and fear. Paul understood his imprisonment as an appointment to the same work, “knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel” (Php 1:17), and his method at Thessalonica was argument from the text, for he “three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures” (Act 17:2).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; Greek apologia (G627), a defence.

expand to see more

Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly, to struggle for; Jude 1:3.

Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, a reasoned answer; 1 Peter 3:15.

Greek agonizomai (G75) — to strive, to contend as in a contest; Jude 1:3.

Greek dialegomai (G1256) — to reason, to discourse, to argue; Acts 17:2.

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, and by extension the body of truth believed; Jude 1:3.

Usage

"“earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — the Malmo Book, 1530."

"“knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel” (Php 1:17) — a canon who turned evangelical."

"“three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures” (Act 17:2) — schoolmaster at Malmo to his death in 1552."
